passage: All of Class 9 in Bhadrachalam seemed to belong to one circle that sat under the neem tree at lunch, and Lavanya had spent a term trying to get into it, laughing at their jokes, buying the same hair clips. It hadn't worked. One Saturday, walking past the old panchayat library, she saw a handwritten sign: "Kolam club. All welcome. Bring chalk." Inside, four people of different ages knelt on the floor around a half-finished pattern. A girl in a green dupatta looked up. "I'm Hafsa. Can you do the curved lines? I always mess them up." Lavanya could, actually; her grandmother had taught her. For two hours nobody asked who she sat with at lunch. They argued about dots and spacing, and Hafsa shared her groundnuts. Walking home with chalk dust on her knees, Lavanya noticed she hadn't once checked what the neem-tree circle was doing.

qa.q: What did the sign outside the panchayat library say to bring?
qa.a: It said to bring chalk.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel walking home with chalk dust on her knees?
qa.a: She felt content and included, so relaxed that she hadn't once checked on the neem-tree circle.

qa.q: Why did the kolam club work where the neem-tree circle didn't?
qa.a: At the club the shared task gave Lavanya a natural role, since she could draw curved lines, so belonging came from doing something together instead of trying to impress.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see Lavanya after that Saturday?
qa.a: Hafsa may be glad to have found someone who can do the curved lines and hope Lavanya comes back.

grounding: Shows a left-out teen finding belonging in a small group built around a shared interest instead of chasing the popular crowd.

passage:
Vasudha's diary, 2:40 am, hostel room 114
Couldn't sleep again. Watched Asif's reels from home: the whole gang at the beach, the chai place near the bus stand, his cousin's wedding. Everyone laughing. I watched the beach one maybe six times.
Then I scrolled through people I don't even know. A girl from my old school in Canada now, perfect apartment, perfect friends. Somebody's birthday dinner. Somebody's new puppy.
It helped, kind of, for a while. Like the room was less quiet. Then I put the phone down and the quiet came back worse, because now I know they're all out there having a life, and I'm here in a room that smells of instant noodles.
Amma messaged at 10: "Eaten?" I sent a thumbs up and nothing else.
Tomorrow I'll go to the canteen properly. Maybe.

qa.q: How many times did Vasudha watch the beach reel?
qa.a: Vasudha watched the beach one maybe six times.

qa.q: What does Vasudha feel after putting the phone down?
qa.a: Vasudha feels lonelier and more left behind, because comparing with others' lives makes the quiet room feel worse.

qa.q: What small turning point is open to Vasudha now?
qa.a: Vasudha could reply properly to Amma or message Asif directly instead of only watching, and actually go to the canteen tomorrow to be near real people.

qa.q: How might Amma feel getting only a thumbs up in reply?
qa.a: Amma may feel a little shut out and worried, sensing something is off but not knowing what to ask.

grounding: Shows a student far from home scrolling at night through others' lives, numbing the ache briefly while comparison deepens it.

subtype: Stage 5: Deepening isolation and low mood [Actor]
passage: The rains had knocked out the power in Uma's rented room in Guwahati for two days, and she hadn't noticed at first because she was mostly asleep. She slept at odd hours now, woke tired, ate biscuits standing up. The rice she had bought a week ago sat unopened. Her phone showed nine missed calls from Vasudha, her friend from the tuition centre. Each one made her stomach twist. What would she even say? That she had skipped classes for ten days? That everyone had enough problems without her being a bother too? It was easier to leave it. Every day she didn't reply made replying feel more impossible. On the third evening someone knocked. "Uma? It's me. I brought khichdi. You don't have to talk." Uma stood behind the door for a long minute, her hand on the latch, before she opened it.

qa.q: How many missed calls from Vasudha did Uma's phone show?
qa.a: Her phone showed nine missed calls from Vasudha.

qa.q: Why does each missed call make Uma's stomach twist?
qa.a: Uma feels ashamed and low, believing she would only be a bother, and the longer she stays silent the more anxious replying feels.

qa.q: What turning point is available now that Vasudha is at the door?
qa.a: Uma can let Vasudha in and accept the khichdi, and with Vasudha's help see a doctor or counsellor about the changes in her sleep, eating and energy.

qa.q: What might Vasudha be feeling as she stands at the door?
qa.a: Vasudha is probably worried and anxious after nine unanswered calls, but she keeps it gentle so Uma doesn't feel pressured.

grounding: Shows sleep, appetite and energy shifting while a person feels a burden and hides from those who care, with silence making reaching out harder.

subtype: Stage 5: Deepening isolation and low mood [Observer]
passage: Deepika pulled her knees up on the hostel terrace and told her senior what had been bothering her. "I'm Deepika, Manoj's lab partner and one floor up, so I notice. First he stopped coming to the mess for dinner. Then he skipped our Friday movie on the terrace, which he started. His room light is on at four. When I asked, he said, 'I'm fine, just busy.' My first idea was to give him a speech about taking care of himself. I didn't. I just knocked on Monday and said, 'Going for chai, want to come? No worries if not.' He said no. I knocked again Wednesday. No. Thursday he came, sat for ten minutes, barely spoke. Friday he came again. It's been three weeks like this, though, and he still looks flat. I think I have to tell him, gently, that talking to the campus doctor or counsellor isn't a big deal."

qa.q: On which day did Manoj finally come for chai?
qa.a: Thursday he came, sat for ten minutes and barely spoke.

qa.q: How does Deepika feel about the change in Manoj?
qa.a: Deepika is worried and uneasy, noticing how much he has pulled back, but she is also patient and hopeful when he joins for chai.

qa.q: What is Deepika doing well, and what is her next step?
qa.a: She offers simple, low-pressure invitations again and again instead of a lecture, and since his low mood has lasted three weeks, she plans to gently suggest the campus doctor or counsellor.

qa.q: What might it be like for Manoj when Deepika keeps knocking?
qa.a: Manoj may feel both awkward and quietly grateful, because saying yes is hard but the steady invitations show someone still wants him there.

grounding: Shows a hostel mate noticing someone who has stopped coming out, offering steady, low-pressure invitations instead of a lecture, and recognising that lasting low mood needs a doctor or counsellor.

passage: I'm Damini, and for most of last year I ate lunch at my desk with the door half closed. People at the office stopped asking. So when Raghav from accounts sent a message to the whole floor, "Anyone want to walk to the new dosa place at one? Zero pressure," I nearly scrolled past it. Then I typed "ok" before I could think too much, and immediately wanted to delete it. At one o'clock I almost didn't get up. My heart was loud the whole way to the lift. There were only three of us: Raghav, a trainee and me. We talked about nothing much, the rain, whether the chutney was too sweet. I laughed once, surprising myself. Walking back, I realised nothing bad had happened. The next Tuesday, when Raghav asked again, I didn't hesitate for as long.

qa.q: Where did Raghav invite people to walk at one?
qa.a: Raghav invited them to walk to the new dosa place at one.

qa.q: How did Damini feel on the way to the lift?
qa.a: Damini felt nervous, with a loud heart, and almost didn't go, but was also a little hopeful.

qa.q: Why did such a small step matter so much for Damini?
qa.a: A short, low-stakes lunch where nothing bad happened rebuilt Damini's belief that contact with people was possible, which made saying yes the next Tuesday easier.

qa.q: How might Raghav experience the lunch walk?
qa.a: Raghav may be pleased someone quiet said yes and glad the zero-pressure message worked, without knowing how big a step it was.

grounding: Shows a person saying yes to a plain, low-stakes invitation and rebuilding the belief that contact is possible.

subtype: Stage 7: Building a few real ties [Response]
passage:
Dear Nandini Akka,
You asked last month if I'd made any friends here in Hyderabad yet. Honestly, when you asked, not really. But something slowly happened.
Every Saturday at seven, the same four of us play badminton at the colony court. I only went because the watchman kept inviting me. Nobody talked much at first. Now after the game we sit on the wall and argue about whose smash was weaker.
On Wednesdays, Imran from the flat below and I cook together, because neither of us can finish a whole pot of sambar alone. Last week he told me about his father's surgery, and I told him about Appa.
It isn't a big group, Akka. Just three or four people I see every week. But when I had fever last month, two of them brought food. I didn't have that a year ago.
Your brother,
Kishore

qa.q: On which day do Kishore and Imran cook together?
qa.a: They cook together on Wednesdays.

qa.q: How does Kishore seem to feel about the new friendships?
qa.a: Kishore feels grateful and a little surprised, quietly proud that these weekly habits turned into real care when the fever came.

qa.q: What made these ties grow, and what could Kishore keep doing?
qa.a: Showing up every week for badminton and the Wednesday cooking let trust build slowly; keeping those routines steady will keep the friendships growing.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Nandini will probably feel relieved and happy that her brother is no longer alone in Hyderabad.

grounding: Shows regular, modest contact such as a weekly game and shared cooking growing into a few real friendships.

passage: The staff room at the call centre emptied at the 3 pm break, and Vidya's old habit was to sit alone and scroll until the buzzer. Her phone's weekly report had said five hours a day. Six weeks ago she had made herself a rule, taped inside her locker: "Online 8 to 9 pm only. Plus one real plan a day." Today's plan was on the sticky note: "Walk with Gurleen, 3 pm." Gurleen from the billing team was already at the door with two cutting chais. They walked around the parking lot twice, complaining about a difficult customer and laughing about the new manager's tie. Vidya's phone buzzed in her pocket once. She left it. At nine that night she did open the video site, watched her usual cooking channel for the full hour, and then plugged the phone in across the room.

qa.q: What was written on today's sticky note?
qa.a: It said: Walk with Gurleen, 3 pm.

qa.q: How does Vidya seem to feel on the walk with Gurleen?
qa.a: Vidya seems relaxed and cheerful, laughing about the manager's tie and calm enough to ignore the buzzing phone.

qa.q: Which parts of Vidya's plan make it work?
qa.a: She set a clear online window and paired it with one real plan each day, so the phone stays a tool for her cooking channel, not a replacement for people.

qa.q: How might Gurleen experience these daily walks?
qa.a: Gurleen probably enjoys them too, a chance to vent about customers and share a laugh during a long shift.

grounding: Shows a person setting a fixed window for online time and pairing it with one offline plan each day, so screens stay a tool rather than a substitute for company.

passage:
Note by the Class 4 teacher, school picnic, Saturday
At the farm gate a brown dog ran out barking. Avni stopped dead and grabbed my sleeve. "My stomach is all tight, Ma'am, my heart is going bang bang, that means it will bite." The dog was chained and stopped well before us, but Avni would not move. Her friend Ira said, "It's tied, Avni, see?" Avni shook her head and cried.
What I did next: I walked Avni to the far side of the bus, where she could still see the dog from a distance, and we breathed slowly together. I told her the tight stomach is her body's alarm, which can ring even when things are safe. I will tell her parents at pickup.

qa.q: What did Avni say her heart was doing?
qa.a: She said her heart was going bang bang.

qa.q: Why was Avni sure the dog would bite?
qa.a: Avni felt terrified, and she took her tight stomach and pounding heart as proof that the dog was dangerous.

qa.q: How did the teacher support Avni at this stage, and what else could help?
qa.a: The teacher gave her distance and slow breathing and explained the body's alarm; later, small, calm practice with gentle dogs could help her learn the alarm isn't always right.

qa.q: How might Ira feel when Avni starts to cry?
qa.a: Ira may feel confused and a little helpless, because to her the chain made it obvious the dog was safe.

grounding: Shows a child's knotted stomach and pounding heart at the sight of a dog, with the body's alarm taken as proof of real danger.

passage:
Note from Tanuja's mother, for the class teacher, Tuesday
On Sunday night Tanuja said her stomach hurt, and on Monday, the day of the maths oral test, she cried that she couldn't go. I let her stay home. An hour after the bus left, she was building a tent with her brother Dhruv and asking for pakoras.
Last night it started earlier. At dinner, before anyone mentioned school, she said, "What if my tummy hurts tomorrow?"
What I did next: this morning I told her I believed her tummy felt bad, that worry can do that, and that she would still go. I walked her to the gate. If the aches keep going or worry me, I'll check with our doctor. Could the oral test be tried again with you nearby?

qa.q: Who did Tanuja build a tent with on Monday?
qa.a: She built a tent with her brother Dhruv.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja's stomach ache disappear soon after the school bus left?
qa.a: The fear of the maths oral test dropped once school was avoided, and she felt relieved, so the ache faded.

qa.q: What turning point did Tanuja's mother choose, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She believed the tummy ache but still sent Tanuja to school with support, which stops avoidance from becoming the safe move while asking the teacher to help.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see Monday?
qa.a: Dhruv probably saw a fun day building a tent with his sister and may not understand why she was home, or wonder why he couldn't stay home too.

grounding: Shows a child's stomach ache keeping her home from a test, the quick relief that follows, and the fear starting earlier the next time.

passage: At the school canteen, Gopika put her tray down across from Siddharth. "You didn't reply in the group. We're going bowling on Saturday." Siddharth shrugged. "Didn't see it." He had seen it; he had muted the chat a week ago. It had started with the history presentation last month. He'd faked a cough and skipped it, and the relief had been huge. Then the group chat felt risky too, all those people who might mention it. Then Saturday outings. Now, when his phone rang, even when it was his uncle, his stomach clenched and he let it ring out. "You've been weird," Gopika said. "Everyone thinks you're angry with us." "I'm not." He meant it. He just wanted them to stop asking. Walking back to class, he took the long way to avoid the corridor where the history teacher sat.

qa.q: What did Siddharth fake to skip the history presentation?
qa.a: He faked a cough and skipped it.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when his phone rang?
qa.a: Siddharth felt anxious, with his stomach clenching, even when it was only his uncle, so he let it ring out.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Siddharth at this stage?
qa.a: He could tell Gopika honestly that he has been anxious, try one small step like replying in the group, and talk to a trusted adult or the school counsellor about the fear.

qa.q: How might Gopika see Siddharth's silence?
qa.a: Gopika and the others read it as anger with them, which leaves Gopika hurt and confused when it is really fear.

grounding: Shows a teenager who avoided one presentation now dodging chats, outings and calls, his safe world shrinking.
